title: Balancing your blood sugar: what actually makes a difference
summary: Fibre, glycaemic load, movement and sleep: ways to support metabolic health.
body_markdown:
A bowl of white rice eaten on its own and a plate combining rice, vegetables, lentils and fish both contain carbohydrates. Yet they can produce very different blood glucose responses.


The amount of carbohydrate matters, of course. But its structure, fibre content, the composition of the meal and even what you've been doing in the hours beforehand all influence how your body processes it.


This is why **healthy blood sugar regulation** matters: understanding what helps your body absorb, use and store glucose efficiently, throughout the day and over the years.


**Why is this important?**


Because our ability to regulate blood glucose and respond effectively to insulin plays a central role in metabolic health.


## Is a rise in blood glucose after a meal a problem?


After a meal containing carbohydrates, digestion releases glucose into the bloodstream. **This rise is entirely normal and physiological:** glucose becomes available to fuel our cells, particularly those in the brain and muscles, or to replenish our energy stores.


In response, the pancreas releases insulin, a hormone that helps the body use and store glucose. Between meals, the liver helps maintain stable blood glucose levels, partly through the action of glucagon.


**What matters is how effectively the body regulates blood glucose** after each meal.


When cells become less sensitive to insulin, the pancreas may need to produce more of it to keep blood glucose within the normal range. Over time, this disruption can contribute to the development of type 2 diabetes and increase cardiovascular risk.


## Glycaemic index and glycaemic load: two different measures


-


The **glycaemic index (GI)** indicates how much a carbohydrate-containing food raises blood glucose compared with a reference food, under standardised conditions.


-


The **glycaemic load (GL)** also takes into account the amount of carbohydrate consumed in a portion.


For example, watermelon has a relatively high glycaemic index but a low glycaemic load for a typical serving, because it contains a lot of water and relatively little carbohydrate.


These measures can be useful, but **glycaemic responses vary considerably between individuals** .


A 2025 study published in *Nature Medicine* used continuous glucose monitoring to measure responses to different carbohydrate foods. On average, rice produced the highest glucose response, but there were substantial differences between participants, partly related to insulin sensitivity. Consuming fibre, protein or fat before the carbohydrate reduced the glucose response in most participants, although the effect was smaller in those with insulin resistance.


Cooking methods, meal composition, physical activity, sleep and insulin sensitivity can all influence this response.


**Ultimately, rather than memorising the glycaemic index of every food, it is more useful to understand the everyday factors that can improve blood glucose regulation.**


## On your plate: four simple strategies


### 1. Choose fibre-rich carbohydrates more often


Fibre, particularly certain types of soluble fibre, slows carbohydrate absorption. It also contributes to satiety, digestive health and overall dietary quality.


Good sources include lentils, chickpeas, beans, oats, wholegrain or sourdough bread made with wholegrain flour, whole grains, vegetables, whole fruit, seeds and nuts.


The World Health Organization recommends that adults consume **at least 25 g of dietary fibre per day (while France's ANSES sets an adequate intake of 30 g per day)** and prioritises whole grains, vegetables, fruit and legumes as the main sources of carbohydrates.


In practice, eating legumes regularly and choosing less refined versions of everyday foods will generally be more beneficial than constantly searching for the food with the lowest glycaemic index.


### 2. Think about the whole meal


Protein, fat and fibre all affect digestion and can influence how quickly glucose enters the bloodstream.


A simple way to build a meal is to include **a generous portion of vegetables, a source of protein, carbohydrates adapted to your appetite and activity level, and quality fats** such as olive oil, nuts or seeds.


For example, a bowl of rice can be combined with vegetables, tofu or fish and a drizzle of olive oil. At breakfast, wholegrain bread with eggs and fruit provides more protein and fibre than bread and jam alone, helping you feel satisfied for longer and potentially moderating the glucose response.


These combinations also help meet nutritional needs and make meals more satisfying. People who are very physically active may naturally need larger portions of carbohydrate-rich foods.


### 3. Consider the structure of your food


Whole fruit and fruit juice both contain sugars, but their physical structure is different. Whole fruit provides fibre and requires more chewing, while juice makes it easy to consume a substantial amount of free sugars quickly.


How finely grains are milled, how foods are cooked and how extensively they are processed can also change how accessible starch is to digestive enzymes. An intact grain, rolled oats and finely milled flour will therefore not necessarily produce the same glucose response.


A useful principle is to **preserve the natural structure of foods** whenever possible, rather than choosing them solely according to the amount of sugar listed on the label.


### 4. Eat enough and build meals that keep you satisfied


Feeling particularly tired after lunch, struggling to concentrate, becoming hungry again soon after eating or craving sugar in the afternoon are all reasons to look more closely at the composition and size of your meals.


However, these sensations are not very specific. A natural dip in alertness occurs in the early afternoon even without eating, and sleep deprivation can make it more pronounced. Feeling sleepy after lunch does not, by itself, indicate a blood glucose problem, although meal composition is one factor worth exploring.


A meal made up mainly of refined carbohydrates, with little protein or fibre, may produce a faster glucose response and leave you feeling hungry again sooner. Conversely, a meal that is too small may simply fail to provide enough energy.


Sleep, stress and physical activity also influence appetite, alertness and blood glucose regulation. Looking at these symptoms in the context of your overall lifestyle is therefore important.


**In practice, if you regularly feel hungry or experience a noticeable energy dip soon after eating, start by looking at what was on your plate:** enough protein? Fibre? A portion size that meets your needs?


A snack may also be appropriate depending on your needs: fruit with plain yoghurt, wholegrain toast with cheese, or a handful of nuts.


The goal is to build meals that provide enough energy, promote lasting satiety and support healthy blood glucose regulation throughout the day.


## Beyond food: lifestyle matters too


### Walk after meals


When muscles contract, they increase glucose uptake, partly through mechanisms that work independently of insulin. A gentle 10–15-minute walk, ideally within 30 minutes after eating, can reduce the immediate post-meal glucose response. The effect tends to be greater when movement begins soon after the meal, although the magnitude varies between individuals.


### Maintain your muscle mass


Muscle is one of the body's major sites for glucose use and storage. Strength training, endurance exercise and daily movement improve the body's ability to handle carbohydrates over time. Regularly breaking up long periods of sitting provides additional benefits.


### Protect your sleep


In a randomised trial involving 38 women, reducing sleep by approximately 1 hour and 20 minutes per night for six weeks increased fasting insulin and an index of insulin resistance, independently of changes in body fat. Other studies have shown that these parameters can return towards normal after sufficient sleep is restored. Sleep duration and regularity are therefore practical factors in metabolic health.


### Consider stress and daily rhythms


Cortisol and other stress hormones influence glucose availability. Circadian rhythms also affect how the body responds to meals. Keeping relatively consistent schedules, allowing enough time for recovery and adapting meals to the demands of the day can all help support metabolic regulation.


Consistent, realistic habits matter more than getting every single day exactly right.


## What can biomarkers tell us?


Blood tests can help explore different aspects of blood glucose regulation: how much glucose is circulating in the blood, its average level over several months, and how much insulin the body is producing.


### Fasting glucose


The amount of glucose in the blood after a period of fasting. A key marker used in diabetes screening.


### HbA1c


Average blood glucose over the previous two to three months, providing insight into longer-term glucose regulation. Results can be distorted by iron-deficiency anaemia (falsely elevated values) or haemolysis (falsely reduced values).


### Fasting insulin


The amount of insulin circulating after an appropriate fasting period. It can provide information about the body's insulin requirements, although there is no universally accepted diagnostic threshold.


### HOMA-IR


An index calculated from fasting glucose and fasting insulin to estimate insulin resistance.


### Triglycerides and HDL cholesterol


Additional indicators of metabolic health and cardiovascular risk.


**At Lucis, we look at these biomarkers together to gain a clearer understanding of your metabolic health.**


For example, normal fasting glucose can coexist with relatively elevated insulin levels. In this situation, the pancreas is producing more insulin to maintain blood glucose within the expected range. This may point towards reduced insulin sensitivity and warrant further investigation in the appropriate clinical context.


Looking at these results alongside HbA1c and lipid markers provides a more complete picture of metabolic health. It helps identify which parameters deserve closer attention and allows their evolution to be monitored over time.
